title: Made on Purpose
passageText: For You formed my inmost being; You knit me together in my mother’s womb. I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Marvelous are Your works, and I know this very well.
bigIdea: You were not an accident or a mistake. God made you on purpose, and He likes what He made.
reflection:
There's a difference between being made and being assembled. A factory assembles a thing fast and forgets it. But the psalm says God knit you together, slow and careful, the way someone makes a blanket they care about. He knew the color of your eyes before anyone else did. He knew the sound of your laugh.

Most of us spend a lot of energy trying to become someone other people will approve of. We change how we talk, how we dress, what we like. But you don't have to earn the right to exist. You already belong to the One who made you, and He has never once been disappointed that He made you.

younger: What is one thing about your body or your personality that you really like, and one thing you sometimes wish was different?
Where do you feel pressure to be someone you're not so people will like you?
If God made you on purpose and is glad He did, how might that change the way you feel walking into school tomorrow?
older: Where do you currently get your sense of being worth something, and what happens to you when that source has a bad week?
What is the difference between an identity you build and an identity you're given?
The psalm says God formed your “inmost being,” the part nobody else sees. Is it a comfort or a little unsettling to be known that well? Why?

activity: Have each person trace their hand on paper, then everyone else writes one true and kind thing about that person inside the hand outline.
prayer: God, thank you for making me on purpose. Help me believe I'm wonderful to you even on days I don't feel it. Amen.

title: When the Lights Go Out
passageText: When I am afraid, I put my trust in You. In God, whose word I praise— in God I trust. I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?
bigIdea: Being scared is not a sin or a failure. The verse doesn't say if I am afraid, it says when.
reflection:
Notice the psalm doesn't pretend fear away. The writer is scared and says so out loud. Then he does something small and brave. He hands the fear to God instead of carrying it alone in the dark. You can trust God while your heart is still pounding.

Kids and grown-ups both get scared, just about different things. It might be a dark room or a test, a friendship falling apart, or a phone call that brings bad news. The promise here isn't that nothing scary will ever happen. The promise is that you will not face it by yourself.

younger: What is something that scares you, even a little, that you've never said out loud?
What do you usually do when you get scared, hide it, get angry, or tell someone?
What would it look like to trust God with a fear this week instead of just trying to feel braver on your own?
older: What are people your age most anxious about right now, and which of those worries do you carry too?
The psalm asks, “What can man do to me?” People can do a lot of harm. What do you think the writer meant?
Is there a fear you've been handling by staying busy or scrolling instead of saying it out loud? Who could you say it to, besides God?

activity: Turn off all the lights, sit in the dark together for one minute, then turn them on and talk about how it felt to not be alone in it.
prayer: God, when I'm afraid I'm going to tell you instead of hiding it. Thank you that I never have to be scared by myself. Amen.

title: The Weight You Put Down
passageText: Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you.
bigIdea: Forgiving someone is not saying what they did was okay. It's choosing to stop making them pay for it.
reflection:
When someone hurts us, it feels fair to hold it against them. We keep a little list. We remember. And the strange thing is, the list gets heavy, and we're the ones who have to carry it. Forgiveness is setting the weight down, not because the other person earned it, but because you don't want to carry it anymore.

The reason the verse gives is that God forgave us first. We've all done things we needed forgiving for. None of us forgives from a high place looking down. We forgive like people who have already been let off a much bigger debt than the one we're holding against someone else.

younger: Is there someone you're a little mad at right now, even a brother or sister in this room?
Has someone ever forgiven you for something, and how did that feel?
What is the difference between forgiving someone and pretending they never hurt you?
older: Is it harder for you to forgive someone who hurt you once in a big way, or someone who keeps hurting you in small ways? Why?
Paul tells us to forgive “just as in Christ God forgave you.” How does remembering what you've been forgiven change the way you see the person you're angry with?
Can you forgive someone and still keep your distance from them? When would that be the wise thing to do?

activity: Have each person hold a heavy book with arms out straight while they name a grudge, then set the book down to feel how forgiveness lightens the load.
prayer: God, you forgave me for a lot. Help me set down the grudges I'm carrying and forgive the way you forgive me. Amen.

title: Counting What You Already Have
passageText: Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.
bigIdea: Thankful people aren't the ones with the most stuff. They're the ones who notice what they have.
reflection:
It's easy to live like we're always one thing short of being happy, one more toy, one more level, one more thing the other kid has. The trouble is that finish line keeps moving, and we never arrive. Gratitude does something different. It stops the chase long enough to look at what is already in our hands.

The verse says give thanks in all circumstances, not for all circumstances. Some days are hard, and we don't have to fake a smile. But even on a hard day there's usually a roof, a meal, a person who loves us, a breath in our lungs. Naming those out loud changes us more than we expect.

younger: Name three things from today you're glad about, even small ones.
What is something you wanted badly last year that you barely think about now?
Why do you think it's so easy to notice what we don't have and so hard to notice what we do?
older: What in your life trains you to want more instead of giving thanks?
Is there a difference between feeling grateful and practicing gratitude? Which one do you control?
If you thanked God for one specific thing every night this week, what would change?

activity: Go around the table and each name one thing you're thankful for, then keep going around until someone can't think of a new one.
prayer: God, thank you for the things I forget to notice. Help me see the good you have already put in my life today. Amen.

title: The Empty Seat
passageText: But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, and you will be blessed. Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.
bigIdea: God notices the person standing alone, and He wants us to walk over there.
reflection:
Jesus was always going to the people everyone else stepped around, like the kid eating lunch alone, the new family at church no one talked to, the person other people whispered about. He didn't wait for them to become popular first. He just went.

Jesus says invite the people who can't pay you back. We usually are kind to people who can do something for us. Real kindness shows up when there's nothing in it for you, when the lonely kid won't make you cooler and might even make you less cool. That's the kind of kindness that looks like God.

younger: Who at your school or in your neighborhood usually gets left out?
Have you ever been the new one or the left out one, and what did you wish someone would do?
What is one risk you could take this week to include someone who can't pay you back?
older: Who is on the outside of your friend group, your team, or your group chat, and what keeps you from bringing them in?
Jesus says to invite people who can't repay you. What kind of payback do we quietly expect for being kind, even if we would never say it?
Jesus says the repayment comes “at the resurrection of the righteous.” Why would He point that far ahead to explain kindness now?

activity: Set one extra empty chair at the table tonight and use it to talk about a real person each of you could invite in this week.
prayer: God, help me see the person standing alone the way you see them. Give me the courage to walk over and say hello. Amen.

title: Why, Not Just What
passageText: But the LORD said to Samuel, “Do not consider his appearance or height, for I have rejected him; the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.”
bigIdea: God cares about why you obey, not just whether you obey.
reflection:
You can do the right thing with a heart that is far away. You can clean your room while hating every second and slamming every drawer. The room gets clean, but something is still off, and you know it. God sees the room and He also sees the slamming.

That's good news. God isn't trying to turn you into a robot who follows orders. He wants your heart. Obeying with a willing heart is harder than just doing the task, but it's the thing that slowly grows you into someone who is good all the way through.

younger: Can you think of a time you did the right thing but with a bad attitude?
Why do you think the why behind what we do matters so much to God?
Is it harder for you to obey your parents, or to obey them without grumbling, and why?
older: Samuel was ready to pick a king by his looks and his height. What do people your age judge each other by first, and what does that miss?
It's possible to do everything right on the outside and still be far from God on the inside. Where do you see that in yourself?
Does it bother you or relieve you that God sees your motives and not just your record? Why?

activity: Play a quick round of Simon Says, then talk about the difference between following a rule because you have to and following someone because you trust them.
prayer: God, you see my heart and not just my hands. Help me obey with a heart that wants to do good. Amen.

title: More Than a Good Teacher
passageText: The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through Him and for Him.
bigIdea: Jesus is more than a kind man from history. He is God you can see.
reflection:
A lot of people are happy to call Jesus a good teacher who said nice things about loving each other. That sounds safe. But the people who knew Him best made a much bigger claim. They said the same Jesus who got tired and hungry and cried at a funeral was the One who made the stars in the first place.

That's either the wildest thing anyone has ever said or it's the most important. You can't file Jesus away as just a wise man once you read what He claimed about Himself. He left us with a real decision.

younger: If you had to describe who Jesus is to a friend who knows nothing, what would you say?
What is the difference between calling Jesus a good teacher and calling Him God?
What is one question about Jesus you've always wondered but never asked?
older: Paul writes, “All things were created through Him and for Him.” What changes if the world was made for Jesus and not for us?
Why do you think it's easier for people to admire Jesus than to obey Him?
If Jesus is “the image of the invisible God,” what does His life show you about God that you might not have guessed?

activity: Each person draws what they picture when they hear the name Jesus, then share the pictures and notice how different they are.
prayer: Jesus, you are more than a teacher in a story. You are God who came close. Help me know you for who you really are. Amen.

title: Talking to Someone Who Is There
passageText: But when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.
bigIdea: When you pray, you're talking to a Father who is listening.
reflection:
Prayer can feel strange, like talking into an empty room. We wonder if anyone is there. But Jesus didn't call God a force or a feeling. He called Him Father, and He told us to talk to Him the way you would talk to a dad who loves you and is right outside the door.

You don't need fancy language, and you don't need to sound holy. A short prayer you mean is better than a long one you don't. God isn't grading your grammar. He wants to hear from you, the same way you'd want to hear from your own kid.

younger: What do you usually pray about, and is there anything you think is too small to pray about?
Have you ever felt like God wasn't listening, and what did you do?
If God already knows everything, why do you think He still wants us to talk to Him?
older: When you pray, who is the audience? God, or some version of yourself watching yourself?
When God seems silent, what do you do with your prayers: stop, keep going, or get angry? What do you think God makes of each?
What are you not saying to God right now?

activity: Whisper a one-sentence prayer to God right now, just in your head, then if you want, say out loud how it felt to talk to someone you can't see.
prayer: God, thank you that I can talk to you any time, anywhere, in regular words. Help me remember you are listening. Amen.

title: Can We Trust This Book?
passageText: All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work.
bigIdea: The Bible is one long true story that has held up under hard questions for a very long time.
reflection:
It's fine to ask whether the Bible is true. God isn't nervous about your questions. The Bible was written down by many people over hundreds of years, on different continents, and it still tells one story that points to Jesus. That's a strange thing to explain away.

It also doesn't flatter the people in it. The heroes lie and run and fail, and the book tells us anyway. Made-up stories usually make the heroes look good. This one tells the truth even when the truth is embarrassing, and that honesty is one reason so many people have trusted it.

younger: What is a question you have about the Bible that you're not sure you're allowed to ask?
Why do you think it matters that the Bible shows its heroes failing?
What would change about how you live if you really believed this book is true?
older: What is the strongest reason you've heard for not trusting the Bible, and what do you make of it?
Paul says Scripture is useful “for conviction, for correction,” and not only for comfort. When has the Bible told you something you didn't want to hear?
What would it take for you to trust the Bible because you have tested it, and not only because your parents do?

activity: Play telephone around the room with a sentence, then talk about how the Bible was carefully copied and checked so the message didn't get scrambled.
prayer: God, I have questions, and I'm glad you are not afraid of them. Help me trust your word and bring you my doubts. Amen.

title: What to Do with the Fire
passageText: My beloved brothers, understand this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger, for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.
bigIdea: Anger isn't always wrong, but it makes a terrible boss.
reflection:
Anger isn't automatically a sin. Even Jesus got angry at things that were truly wrong. The problem is that anger wants to be in charge, and it's a loud, fast, foolish leader. It tells you to say the thing you can't take back and slam the door before you have thought for even a second.

James gives us a speed limit: quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to get angry. Not never angry, just slow. Most of the damage we do happens in the first ten seconds, before our brain catches up to our mouth. Learning to wait those ten seconds is one of the most grown-up things a person can do, and most grown-ups are still working on it.

younger: What is something that makes you angry faster than almost anything else?
What do you tend to do when you're angry, yell, go quiet, or slam something?
What is one thing you could do in the first ten seconds of being angry to slow yourself down?
older: When you get angry, is it usually about something truly wrong, or about something that got in your way? How can you tell the difference?
James says human anger does not bring about the righteousness God desires. Why does anger feel so right in the moment?
Online, people are quick to speak and slow to listen. What would doing the opposite look like in a group chat or a comment section?

activity: Practice taking five slow breaths together, then agree on a family signal anyone can use to say I need ten seconds before I respond.
prayer: God, my anger isn't a good boss. Help me be quick to listen and slow to blow up, even when I really want to. Amen.

grownups.line: If your own temper frightens you or the people you live with, start here.

title: Where Your Eyes Go
passageText: Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is admirable—if anything is excellent or praiseworthy—think on these things.
bigIdea: What you keep looking at slowly becomes what you think about, and what you think about becomes who you are.
reflection:
Screens aren't evil, and this isn't a lecture about how phones are ruining everything. But your attention is one of the most valuable things you own, and a lot of very smart people are paid to keep you staring as long as possible. It's worth asking who is deciding where your eyes go, you or the screen.

The verse works more like a question than a list of rules. After an hour on a screen, do you feel more true, more honorable, more lovely, or just more tired and a little emptier? Both kids and parents in this room know that feeling. The goal isn't zero screens. The goal is to be the one steering.

younger: How do you usually feel after a long time on a screen, better or worse?
What is one thing you love doing that has nothing to do with a screen?
If a screen is steering your attention instead of you, who really gets to decide what you become?
older: What do you scroll past every day that you would never choose to think about if you were deciding on purpose?
Paul's list says true, honorable, right, pure, lovely, admirable. Which of those is hardest to find in your feed, and why?
If someone looked at your screen time for one week, what would they guess you love most? Would they be right?

activity: Put every phone and device in a basket in the middle of the room for the rest of this devotion, then do something together with the time you just got back.
prayer: God, my attention matters to you. Help me steer my eyes toward what is good instead of letting a screen steer them for me. Amen.

title: The Towel and the Basin
passageText: For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.
bigIdea: In God's family, the great ones aren't the ones being waited on. They're the ones doing the serving.
reflection:
The night before He died, Jesus took a towel and washed His friends' dirty feet, the job that belonged to the lowest servant in the house. The King of everything knelt on the floor. He didn't have to. That's what love looks like when it stops talking and starts moving.

We usually want to be the one who is served, the one who gets the biggest piece and the most credit. Jesus flips it. He says the one who wants to be great must be the one who serves. Nobody is more like Jesus than the person doing the serving.

younger: Who serves you every day in ways you might not even notice?
What is a job in this house nobody likes to do, and could you do it without being asked?
Why do you think Jesus, who could have done anything, chose to wash dirty feet?
older: Who gets noticed for serving at your school or on your team, and who does the work nobody sees?
Jesus said He came “to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.” Why do you think He tied serving to dying?
Where in this house do you expect to be served without thinking about it, and what would it look like to change that this week?

activity: Each person secretly does one helpful thing for someone else in the family today without telling them, and see if it gets noticed.
prayer: Jesus, you knelt with a towel when you had every right to be served. Help me look for ways to serve instead of waiting to be served. Amen.
